clinicalPearls: The classic combination is ipsilateral optic atrophy with contralateral papilloedema, caused by a slow-growing frontal or olfactory groove mass
The ipsilateral optic atrophy results from direct compression of that optic nerve, while raised intracranial pressure produces papilloedema in the opposite eye
Anosmia is frequently associated when an olfactory groove or subfrontal meningioma is the cause
Central scotoma and reduced acuity are typical in the atrophic eye, while the swollen disc eye may retain good vision initially
A compressed, already-atrophic optic nerve cannot swell, which is why papilloedema fails to develop on that side
The commonest underlying lesions are olfactory groove and sphenoid wing meningiomas and frontal lobe tumours
Pseudo-Foster Kennedy syndrome describes a similar disc appearance from sequential ischaemic optic neuropathy without a mass
reference.pathophysiology: A slowly enlarging frontal lobe or subfrontal skull base tumour, classically an olfactory groove or sphenoid wing meningioma, directly compresses one optic nerve to produce optic atrophy on that side. As the tumour grows it eventually raises intracranial pressure, which is transmitted to the contralateral optic nerve head causing papilloedema; the already-atrophic nerve on the tumour side cannot swell. Involvement of the olfactory tract explains the frequent anosmia. The sequence reflects the interplay between local compressive atrophy and generalised pressure-driven disc swelling.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudo-Foster Kennedy syndrome from sequential anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
Bilateral papilloedema from idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Bilateral optic atrophy from other compressive or toxic causes
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain with contrast focused on the anterior cranial fossa and skull base
Formal visual field testing of both eyes
Optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve heads and retinal nerve fibre layer
Fundus photography to document disc appearances
redFlags: Imaging evidence of a large frontal or skull base tumour requiring neurosurgical referral
Progressive visual loss in the atrophic eye or new swelling in the fellow eye
Features of raised intracranial pressure such as headache and vomiting
Cognitive or behavioural change suggesting frontal lobe involvement
reference.prognosis: Vision in the atrophic eye is often permanently reduced, but timely resection of the causal tumour can relieve pressure and preserve or improve vision in the fellow eye; overall outcome depends on tumour size and resectability.
pitfalls: Mistaking the picture for pseudo-Foster Kennedy syndrome and missing a treatable mass
Failing to test olfaction, which can point to an olfactory groove tumour
Attributing the atrophic disc to old optic neuritis without imaging
Delaying neuroimaging in a patient with asymmetric disc findings
management: Neurosurgical resection of the causative subfrontal or olfactory-groove meningioma or frontal tumour is the definitive treatment and relieves the raised intracranial pressure threatening the fellow eye
Use corticosteroids perioperatively to reduce peritumoural oedema and control raised intracranial pressure
Offer stereotactic radiosurgery or fractionated radiotherapy for unresectable, residual or recurrent tumour
Monitor both optic nerves with serial visual fields, acuity and optical coherence tomography, prioritising preservation of vision in the papilloedematous eye
Provide low-vision support and rehabilitation for the permanently atrophic eye
Undertake interval surveillance imaging for tumour recurrence
Coordinate care across neurosurgery, neuro-ophthalmology and oncology
